title: Lay Dominicans
hook: laypeople who pray, study and share

segments.voice: Yesterday, Lacordaire, the preacher who came home in a white habit and brought the friars back to France. Your line was back to france. Where did you bring a kindness back into a conversation? Day one thousand two hundred forty-three.

A Tuesday evening in a parish hall. Folding chairs, a coffee urn, a plate of store-bought cookies. Around the table: a nurse still in scrubs, a retired mechanic, a college student, a grandmother with a well-thumbed Bible full of sticky notes. They open with a psalm, prayed back and forth across the table. Then someone reads a short passage, and they argue about it, politely, for an hour. Nobody here wears a habit. Nobody lives in a friary. Everyone goes home to a mortgage or a roommate or a sink full of dishes. And every one of them, by promise, belongs to the Order of Preachers. Today's word is what they are.
screen: `A PARISH HALL ON A TUESDAY.` → `A PSALM, A PASSAGE, AN ARGUMENT.` → `NO HABITS. ALL DOMINICANS.`

segments.voice: Lay Dominicans are laypeople, married or single, with ordinary jobs, who make a promise to live by the Dominican way inside an ordinary life. The Dominicans speak of themselves as a family with several branches: friars, cloistered nuns, sisters in active work, and laypeople. Same motto, same founder, different kitchens. What do the laypeople actually do? The same three things this whole stretch of days keeps circling. Pray: a lay Dominican may take up part of the Church's daily prayer, the psalms of morning or evening. Study: not for a degree, but because Dominicans hold that you can't share what you haven't chewed on. And share, which is the surprising part, because the order's name is preachers. A layperson doesn't preach from a pulpit at Mass. So where? At work, at home, over a fence, in how they answer a hard question from a teenager. Jesus says, in the Douay-Rheims: "So let your light shine before men, that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father who is in heaven." A light doesn't give a speech. It just shines where it is. That's the lay preacher's pulpit: wherever they already stand. And they don't do it alone. The fraternity, the small local group, meets to pray and study together, because a question argued over with friends gets sharper than one carried by yourself. Some weeks, that might be the whole of it: one psalm, one page, one conversation, and a life that quietly says what it learned.
screen: `A PROMISE, LIVED IN AN ORDINARY LIFE.` · `ONE FAMILY: FRIARS, NUNS, SISTERS, LAITY.` · `PRAY, STUDY, SHARE.` · `THE PULPIT IS WHERE YOU STAND.` · then, large: `SO LET YOUR LIGHT SHINE BEFORE MEN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find your study group, or the start of one. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind two or three people you could read something with: a friend, a sibling, a coworker, a neighbor, someone at a parish if you belong to one. Pick one. Then pick one short thing worth reading together, a psalm, a Gospel passage, a single page of anything that matters to you both. Hold the picture of the two of you at a table with it. If you pray, you can ask for a good companion in learning. The bell holds the time.
Lay Dominicans. Laypeople who promise to live the Dominican way at home and at work: praying, studying together, and sharing what they learn. Today's word.

Your line: lay preachers. Their pulpit is wherever they already stand. Today, send one message to the person you pictured, and ask if they'd read one short thing with you. Day one thousand two hundred forty-three.

howItsDone: Lay Dominicans gather in local fraternities, meeting to pray part of the Liturgy of the Hours, study together and plan works of service; after a time of formation, members make a promise to live by the order's rule for the laity.

notes: Confirm the description of lay Dominicans: laypeople (married or single) who, after formation, make a promise (not vows) and belong to local fraternities; the 'Dominican family' language (friars, nuns, apostolic sisters, laity).
'A lay Dominican often takes up part of the Church's daily prayer' (Liturgy of the Hours, morning and evening prayer): confirm against the Rule of the Lay Fraternities.
The voice notes laypeople do not preach the homily at Mass (reserved to clergy); confirm phrasing.
The hook is an invented, typical scene, not a specific fraternity.
Day 1238 already covered Catherine of Siena as a mantellata; this day does not repeat her. Day 1244 (Frassati) is not taught here.
